source_document.body:
Asset-tracking company Band24 is seeking businesses to test Terra, a new tracker combining Bluetooth, cellular and satellite connectivity, ahead of a Nov. 13 deadline for its early-access program. The device is designed to help logistics operators maintain visibility into trailers, shipping containers and other equipment in areas with limited network coverage, with commercial availability planned for early 2027. Selected participants are expected to receive their devices in December, though Band24 has not set an exact delivery date.
The company announced Terra on Oct. 6, saying it can track asset location, movement, dwell time, temperature, humidity and tampering. Band24 has opened an early-access program, with selected participants expected to receive devices in December.
“Every business with physical assets has felt this same pain — you can see your equipment until the exact moment it matters most, and then it’s gone dark,” Band24 co-founder and CEO Patrick Patel said in the announcement.
The launch comes as cargo theft continues to be a problem . Verisk’s CargoNet recorded 2,646 confirmed cargo thefts across the United States and Canada in 2025, an 18% increase from 2024. Estimated losses reached nearly $725 million, up 60%, while the average value per theft climbed to $273,990.
Combining three networks
Terra combines Bluetooth, LTE-M cellular and satellite connectivity through Hubble Network’s low-Earth-orbit satellite network.
The device is designed to use a terrestrial Bluetooth network of more than 100 million crowdsourced access points for routine updates and location determination, LTE-M cellular connectivity when coverage is available, and Hubble’s satellite network when the other two networks are unavailable. Hubble’s satellite technology allows Bluetooth Low Energy devices to send small data packets directly to passing satellites using their existing Bluetooth radios, without requiring a dedicated satellite modem.
Band24 says Terra can return an on-demand location update in about a minute when cellular or terrestrial Bluetooth connectivity is available. Outside those networks, the device relies on satellite transmissions when a Hubble satellite passes overhead, meaning updates follow the satellite’s schedule rather than an on-demand clock. Band24 said satellite performance is expected to improve as Hubble expands its constellation. Hubble reported six satellites in low-Earth orbit as of Sept. 23, 2026.
Terra determines location using a combination of GPS, Wi-Fi localization and a terrestrial network of more than 100 million crowdsourced Bluetooth access points, according to Band24. Hubble’s satellite network provides coarse location information when other methods are unavailable. The device selects when to report and which network to use based on factors including LTE availability, nearby Bluetooth access points and sensor inputs.
The distinction between on-demand and satellite reporting could matter to fleet operators that need to locate equipment quickly in remote areas. Band24 has not provided location-accuracy figures or data on satellite reporting reliability.
Testing and performance
Terra remains in testing and development as Band24 works through regulatory certification ahead of commercial shipment.
Band24 estimates the device’s battery life at four years, though the company said measurements are ongoing and the estimate remains directional. It attributes the expected battery life to its multi-network strategy, which selects a power-efficient connection for each update, low-power wireless technology and on-demand reporting that allows the device to remain inactive between check-ins.
The enclosure carries an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. Terra will connect to Band24’s existing Ranger dashboard and Events API, and users will be able to activate and assign devices using an NFC-enabled smartphone.
Pricing and availability
Band24 has not announced Terra’s hardware price or subscription costs, saying it plans to share pricing closer to general availability. The device will be licensed per unit and will not require customers to purchase hubs or build private networks. The company expects its combination of three connectivity options and multi-year battery life to be competitively priced, but has not provided figures for comparing its total cost with existing trackers.
Why this matters
Freight operators often have limited visibility into trailers, containers and other equipment when they move beyond cellular coverage or between facilities. Terra aims to address those gaps by combining Bluetooth, cellular and satellite connectivity in a single battery-powered tracker. Its value for the logistics industry will depend on whether satellite reporting is frequent and reliable enough to locate assets when needed, as well as the device’s cost and battery life compared with existing tracking options.
